mappings.note: the Bharat Mata image is one of LO-1's icons of collective belonging; nothing here concerns method or the war
the Khilafat Committee's formation and its object (defending the Khalifa against the post-war treaty) is precisely the trigger chain LO-3 names
the Swaraj flag and carrying it in defiance is a symbol of shared nationhood (LO-1); that Gandhiji designed it does not make the question one about the effectiveness of his method
the Hind Swaraj argument -- British rule survives on Indian cooperation, so withdraw it -- is the reasoning behind the strategy, LO-2, not the grievance that triggered it
Bankim's Vande Mataram and the Bharat Mata figure are the cultural material of LO-1; he was not a leader of the movements Gandhiji organised, so LO-2 does not apply
three reasons for choosing the salt tax is the choice of issue -- the strategy in LO-2; who then joined would be LO-1
Natesa Sastri's folk-tale collection and his view of folklore as national literature belong to the cultural making of belonging, LO-1
the Awadh peasants' own demands (revenue cut, end of begar, social boycott of landlords) is a rural facet of the movement, LO-1
Ambedkar's Depressed Classes Association and its demand for separate electorates is another leader's strategy (LO-2); dalits' thin participation in the movement would be LO-1
the Jallianwala Bagh massacre is the post-war repression LO-3 traces into Khilafat and Non-Cooperation
relaunching after the Second Round Table Conference failed is a decision about the campaign, LO-2; LO-3's reach stops at the Non-Cooperation trigger

the 1935 Act and the Cripps Mission fall outside this chapter's span and the frame has no outcome for colonial constitutional policy; LO-2 is the nearest because the Congress's rejection of both is a leaders' decision -- a stretched fit

the Chittagong revolutionaries and Pritilata Wadedar are women entering the national movement, a facet under LO-1; the armed path was outside the movements Gandhiji organised, so LO-2 does not cover it
war expenditure, customs and income tax is the economic effect of the First World War that LO-3 asks to be summarised -- the plainest LO-3 item in the bank
the movement's regional reach into the Madras Presidency, with its own leaders and institutions, is LO-1's spread of belonging rather than a judgement on Gandhian method
three reasons for calling the movement off in 1922 is an evaluation of the strategy's limits, LO-2
read as Gandhiji's own social programme it sits with LO-2, as item 48 does; but the keyed answer is a civics list (communalism, casteism, unjust laws) with no anchor in this chapter -- a weak fit
the three causes given are Rowlatt, Jallianwala Bagh and Khilafat -- exactly the post-war chain LO-3 names as triggering Non-Cooperation

causes of Civil Disobedience (salt tax, Simon, Purna Swaraj) cannot use LO-3, which is restricted to the First World War and the Khilafat/Non-Cooperation trigger; they are the provocations Congress answered with a new campaign, so LO-2
Assam plantation workers reading swaraj as the right to leave the garden is the clearest case of a group's own meaning for the nation -- LO-1
how the movement unfolded in the towns is a roll-call of who acted (students, teachers, lawyers, merchants), LO-1; what the boycott achieved economically would be LO-2
the war's economic and political implications for India is LO-3 word for word
the poor peasantry's role is which group gave the movement its mass character, LO-1; Gandhiji's choice of the salt demand appears only as background
the Lucknow Pact is Congress-League and moderate-extremist unity, i.e. a step towards collective belonging (LO-1); it is not in this NCERT chapter at all, so the fit is by substance, not by text
the industrialists' and traders' part in the struggle is a social group's participation, LO-1; the boycott's measured economic effect would move it to LO-2
